meta.title: Irish A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Irish → English (see the Irish, recall the meaning) and English → Irish (see an English meaning, recall the Irish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words of Irish (Gaeilge) for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to communicate in simple and routine tasks requiring a simple and direct exchange of information on familiar and routine matters, and to describe in simple terms aspects of their background, immediate environment and matters in areas of immediate need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Irish has a graded examination at these levels — the Teastas Eorpach na Gaeilge (TEG) of Maynooth University — whose syllabuses describe each level but do not publish a complete word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 378 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the seasons and dates, more numbers and the numbers for counting people, the land and nature, the weather, animals, clothes, the home and the kitchen, food and cooking, work and jobs, school, travel and transport, the town, health and the body, feelings, people and neighbours, letters, the phone and the news, shopping, free time and sport, the everyday verbs of these, describing things and people, time words, and the words that join one clause to the next — and the other 372 are the commonest remaining words of written Irish, counted over the articles of the Irish-language Wikipedia by the WHOLE word: every form of a noun or a verb added together, and every spelling its initial mutations give it (bean, bhean, mbean). No subtitle frequency list exists for Irish, and an encyclopaedia's commonest words lean towards history, places and people, which is why the deck leads with the hand-written vocabulary. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 509 nouns carry their gender, which decides how the article changes them (an fear, an bhean), and show the noun with the article, its genitive and its plural (an teach, tí, tithe); the 101 verbs are headed by the imperative, the form Irish dictionaries list a verb by (déan, "do"), and show their present, past, future and verbal noun (déanann, rinne, déanfaidh, déanamh). Behind the All forms fold a verb's tenses go by person, a noun shows its lenited and eclipsed forms (theach, dteach) and a preposition its forms with a pronoun (liom, leat, leis). The spelling is the Official Standard (An Caighdeán Oifigiúil) as Wiktionary gives it. Real example sentences come with 300 of the 750 words, three apiece for 107 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword; few devices have an Irish voice, so the speaker may be silent. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Irish Wikipedia (ga.wikipedia.org), its articles as of 1 November 2026, counted for this deck (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
